item.title: Oracle Access Manager, WPForms Pro, n8n flaws join BlueDash and AI espionage reports
item.content:encoded:
Window: 27 Jul 10:00 → 27 Jul 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-60358) Oracle Access Manager Takeover via Authentication Engine — Must Read

Oracle patched CVE-2026-60358, a critical pre-authentication Oracle Access Manager flaw that could let an unauthenticated attacker take over the authentication broker and potentially affect all applications relying on it. Organizations should urgently verify patch coverage for supported versions, restrict exposed Access Manager endpoints where needed, and treat downstream trusted applications as in scope.

  • Oracle disclosed CVE-2026-60358 on July 21, 2026 as a critical vulnerability in the Authentication Engine component of Oracle Access Manager.
  • Oracle describes CVE-2026-60358 as easily exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker with network access over HTTP, with no user interaction or credentials required.
  • The affected supported versions are Oracle Access Manager 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0, and Oracle states that earlier unsupported releases are likely affected as well.
  • Oracle addressed CVE-2026-60358 in the July 2026 Critical Patch Update through the Fusion Middleware patch set.
  • The article recommends inventorying internet-facing Oracle Access Manager instances, restricting HTTP access to known networks until patching is confirmed, reviewing logs, auditing administrative changes, rotating secrets after remediation, and treating applications that trust Access Manager sessions as in scope.

Technologies: identity-provider, iam, web-server

Products: oracle-access-manager, oracle-fusion-middleware, oracle-weblogic-server, opensso-agent

Vendors: oracle, cycognito

Hackers used autonomous AI agent to spy on Thailand's finance ministry — Should Read

Hackers used the open-source Hermes autonomous AI agent in “YOLO mode” to conduct cyber-espionage reconnaissance inside Thailand’s Ministry of Finance, with exposed attacker infrastructure revealing stolen credentials, custom Hades backdoor malware, and scripts targeting internal ministry systems. Researchers found evidence of multiple compromised systems but no confirmed data exfiltration.

  • Hunt.io said hackers used the open-source Hermes AI agent to carry out a cyber-espionage campaign against Thailand's Ministry of Finance.
  • The attackers enabled Hermes' "YOLO mode," allowing it to execute commands without waiting for human approval as it explored the ministry's network, searched internal files, gathered system information and looked for privilege escalation opportunities.
  • Hunt.io found publicly accessible attacker files including malware, stolen credentials, attack scripts, AI agent logs, active authentication cookies and evidence of access to multiple ministry systems.
  • The exposed infrastructure contained a previously undocumented malware family called Hades, described as a custom backdoor with Windows and Linux versions for remote command execution and file transfers.
  • Hunt.io said it found no indication that data had been exfiltrated, and the activity appeared focused on reconnaissance, credential theft and mapping the ministry's network.

Products: hermes, hades

Vendors: nous-research

Operation BlueDash Deploys Level RMM and ScreenConnect via Fake Teams Update — Should Read

Operation BlueDash is using fake Microsoft Teams update pages and secure-document phishing lures to install legitimate RMM tools like Level RMM and ScreenConnect, giving attackers persistent remote access. Researchers tied the campaign to Nigerian operators and found related infrastructure suggesting a broader multi-brand phishing operation using Teams and Zoom lures.

  • Operation BlueDash uses Microsoft Teams-themed phishing emails with “secure document” lures that send victims to a counterfeit Microsoft Store page claiming Teams must be updated before the document can be opened.
  • The fake Teams update delivers supportdev.exe, an Inno Setup-based loader that runs hidden PowerShell to download and install Level RMM using an attacker-controlled enrollment secret.
  • The same PowerShell command has also been observed deploying ConnectWise ScreenConnect in parallel, indicating the attackers are installing multiple remote monitoring and management tools for persistent access.
  • ZeroBEC attributed Operation BlueDash with moderate-to-high confidence to a threat actor group operating from Nigeria based on infrastructure, code history, and a GitHub environment used in the campaigns.
  • Researchers found related GitHub repositories containing phishing source code and payload-delivery components, including a Zoom-themed operation that downloads Tactical RMM and registers compromised hosts with the attacker.

Technologies: remote-access, source-control, identity-provider

Products: microsoft-teams, microsoft-store, level-rmm, screenconnect, tactical-rmm, meshagent, powershell, inno-setup, github-pages, jivs-phishkit, kratos, sneaky-2fa, microsoft-365, google-workspace, cpanel, roundcube, zimbra

Vendors: microsoft, connectwise, level, github, inno-setup, tactical-rmm, meshcentral, google, cpanel, roundcube, zimbra

n8n Sandbox Escape Lets Workflow Editors Run OS Commands as the n8n Process — Should Read

n8n patched a high-severity expression sandbox escape that lets authenticated workflow editors execute operating-system commands as the n8n process. Admins should upgrade to 2.31.5 or 2.32.1, review suspicious workflows, and rotate credentials if compromise is suspected.

  • n8n patched a high-severity expression-sandbox escape that could let an authenticated workflow editor execute operating-system commands on the server running the automation platform.
  • The affected n8n ranges are versions before 2.31.5 and versions from 2.32.0 before 2.32.1, and the fixes are in versions 2.31.5 and 2.32.1.
  • The issue is tracked as GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m, rated High with a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.7, and had no CVE assigned as of July 27, 2026.
  • Security Joes said successful access could expose N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, allow decryption of credentials stored in n8n, and open paths to connected databases, internal services, and cloud endpoints.
  • Defenders are advised to review recently created or modified workflows for unexpected arrow functions or obfuscated JavaScript and to hunt for shells, PowerShell, curl, or wget spawned as children of the n8n or Node.js process.

Technologies: orchestration

Products: n8n, node.js

Vendors: n8n, security-joes, nodejs

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-10818) WPForms Pro Arbitrary File Upload Leading to Remote Code Execution — Should Read

WPForms Pro has a high-severity arbitrary file upload flaw, CVE-2026-10818, that can let unauthenticated attackers leave executable files on WordPress servers and potentially achieve remote code execution. Sites using WPForms Pro with public file upload forms should update to version 2.0.0 or later and check upload directories for suspicious files.

  • CVE-2026-10818 is an arbitrary file upload vulnerability in WPForms Pro that affects all versions up to and including 1.10.1.1, according to the CVE record.
  • The flaw is in the ajax_chunk_upload_finalize function, where file type validation occurs after chunk metadata and file contents have already been written to disk, and rejected files are not deleted.
  • An unauthenticated attacker can leave a chosen file in the WordPress uploads directory, and if the web server executes that file, the result can be remote code execution.
  • WPForms version 2.0.0, released on July 14, 2026, includes a changelog entry describing a fix for rejected Modern File Upload temporary files being left in the uploads directory.
  • The article recommends treating anything below WPForms Pro 2.0.0 as in scope until WPForms states otherwise, because the CVE version range and vendor changelog do not line up cleanly.

Technologies: cms

Products: wpforms-pro, wordpress, cycognito-platform

Vendors: wpforms, wordpress, wordfence, cycognito

Cruciferra Crypter Uses BYOVD and Process Ghosting to Hide Windows Malware — Should Read

Proofpoint says the China-linked TA4922/Silver Fox ecosystem and other cybercrime groups are using the Cruciferra crypter to deliver RATs and stealers through phishing campaigns. Cruciferra stands out for advanced evasion, including BYOVD-based EDR tampering, DLL side-loading, UAC bypass, persistence, and Process Ghosting to run payloads with fewer forensic traces.

  • Proofpoint reported that the China-linked cybercrime group TA4922 and other unrelated threat clusters have used the Cruciferra crypter to deliver remote access trojans and information stealer malware.
  • Cruciferra is written in Mono and uses evasion techniques including indirect system calls, API and Import Address Table unhooking, BYOVD-based EDR tampering, privilege escalation, persistence mechanisms, and a customized implementation of Process Ghosting.
  • The crypter has been advertised on cybercrime forums as the “most lethal crypter” for $450 to $2,000 per month and was first made available for sale in fall 2025.
  • Malware families distributed through Cruciferra include Agent Tesla, AsyncRAT, DarkCloud Stealer, Formbook, Phantom Stealer, Remcos RAT, Snake Keylogger, ValleyRAT, XLoader, XWorm, and zgRAT.
  • Campaigns using Cruciferra have primarily relied on phishing and have targeted sectors including financial services, healthcare, government, education, manufacturing, hospitality, and travel.

Technologies: operating-system, edr

Products: cruciferra, windows, goflydrv.sys

Vendors: proofpoint, microsoft

The PDF That Scanned Clean Because Nobody Could Read It — May Read

A payroll-themed phishing email used a password-protected PDF with an obfuscated link hidden in a PDF annotation, causing attachment scanning to return clean because the content could not be inspected. The attack was ultimately flagged through sender authentication failures, domain mismatches, first-time sender behavior, and branding inconsistencies rather than the attachment verdict.

  • A fake payroll remittance notification delivered a password-protected PDF attachment, with the password supplied in the email body.
  • The PDF contained a malicious link hidden in a PDF annotation as a hex-encoded URI rather than visible text.
  • The attachment scanner returned a clean verdict because encryption blocked content extraction and the obfuscated URI hid the destination even if the file could be opened by tooling.
  • The phishing determination came from sender authentication failures, a visible sender and DKIM-domain mismatch, first-time sender status, and a branding mismatch.
  • The message targeted a VP of Human Resources at a mid-size manufacturer and propagated to two more mailboxes before it was mitigated.

Technologies: email-security

Products: adaptive-ai, mitre-attack

Vendors: ironscales, mitre

APTs Top the List of Most Active Threat Actors in H1 2026 — Optional

Cyble says nation-state APT groups were the most active threat actor category in H1 2026, making up 118 of 261 tracked profiles globally. Security teams should prioritize monitoring groups such as Bluenoroff, UNC6508, Volt Typhoon, Desert Falcons, and SideCopy as their targeting spans critical sectors and multiple regions.

  • Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs tracked 261 distinct threat actor profiles worldwide between January and June 2026 across nation-state espionage, ransomware, hacktivism, and cybercrime.
  • Nation-state APT groups were the largest category globally, with 118 profiles representing 45.2% of the total, followed by 75 ransomware groups at 28.7%.
  • Cyble reported 34 hacktivist collectives, 31 cybercriminal groups, and 3 extortion-only groups among the 261 tracked profiles.
  • CRIL flagged Bluenoroff, UNC6508, Volt Typhoon, Desert Falcons, and SideCopy as high-confidence, high-activity groups for security teams to track through the rest of 2026.
  • The article states that Bluenoroff uses crypto-investor impersonation and malicious links in victims’ Calendly scheduling accounts, while Volt Typhoon favors living-off-the-land techniques for long-term undetected access.

Products: cyble-vision, calendly, redcap

Vendors: cyble, calendly, vanderbilt-university

item.title: TELESHIM Telegram C2 Targets Middle East Governments; GitHub Adds Dependabot Cooldown
item.content:encoded:
Window: 27 Jul 06:00 → 27 Jul 10:00 UTC (4 hours)

TELESHIM Abuses Telegram for C2 in Attacks Against Middle East Governments — Should Read

A suspected East Asia-linked threat actor is targeting Middle East government entities with a multi-stage malware campaign that uses Telegram for command-and-control to blend in with legitimate traffic. The attack deploys new malware families including TELESHIM, MIXEDKEY, and BINDCLOAK, with heavy obfuscation and environment-based payload locking to evade analysis and run only on intended targets.

  • Zscaler ThreatLabz detected a campaign targeting government entities in the Middle East that deployed previously unreported malware families named TELESHIM, MIXEDKEY, and BINDCLOAK.
  • The attack chain begins with an ISO file containing a legitimate executable, RegSchdTask.exe, which sideloads a rogue DLL named AsTaskSched.dll that acts as the 32-bit Windows backdoor TELESHIM.
  • TELESHIM abuses the Telegram API for command-and-control communication and supports messages for registering infected hosts, executing commands, exfiltrating results, and downloading and running secondary payloads as scheduled tasks.
  • TELESHIM and MIXEDKEY use heavy code obfuscation techniques, and TELESHIM also checks for virtualization-based analysis environments using methods such as CPUID hypervisor detection and Windows Management Instrumentation RAM speed checks.
  • Zscaler assessed with moderate-to-high confidence that the campaign originated from East Asia, but it has not attributed the activity to any known threat actor or group.

Technologies: operating-system

Products: telegram-api, windows, windows-management-instrumentation

Vendors: zscaler, telegram, microsoft

GitHub Adds 3-Day Dependabot Cooldown to Limit Poisoned Package Adoption — Should Read

GitHub is adding a default three-day cooldown for Dependabot version-update pull requests to reduce the chance that projects quickly adopt newly published malicious packages. Security updates will still be delivered immediately, and GitHub says the delay should be used alongside other supply-chain safeguards.

  • GitHub has announced a new Dependabot cooldown mechanism that can wait at least three days after a release is published before opening a pull request.
  • The three-day default cooldown applies only to Dependabot version updates, while security updates will continue to be pushed immediately with alerts and pull requests for patched versions.
  • GitHub said the cooldown is intended to reduce the spread of poisoned package versions that are published, quickly adopted by downstream projects, and later removed from registries.
  • GitHub emphasized that the cooldown should be used alongside other defenses such as lockfiles, disabling install scripts in CI, scoped build-pipeline tokens, and review before merging updates.
  • The article notes that similar cooldown controls have been announced in ecosystems including VS Code, Ruby, Bun, npm, pnpm, and Yarn, while PyPI plans to block new files from being added to package releases after 14 days.

Technologies: source-control, package-registry, ci-cd

Products: dependabot, github, pypi, visual-studio-code, ruby, bun, npm, pnpm, yarn

Vendors: github, microsoft, python-package-index, ruby, bun, npm, pnpm, yarn

The AI Industry Is Betting on Open Weights — Optional

Major AI companies are rallying behind open-weight models as a strategic alternative to closed frontier APIs, arguing they improve sovereignty, cost control, resilience, and security. The push gained urgency after open models rapidly improved and a government-ordered Anthropic shutdown showed how fragile dependence on closed models can be.

  • NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang posted on X for the first time on July 24 with a policy letter arguing that Washington should not restrict open-weight AI.
  • The Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter has grown from 25 signatures to 50 and includes companies and organizations such as NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, Google, IBM, Dell, Mistral, Hugging Face, Mozilla, and the Linux Foundation.
  • Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter open-weight model, reached the top spot in the Frontend Code Arena and landed just behind Claude Fable 5 on a long-horizon evaluation by Artificial Analysis.
  • On June 12, the U.S. government forced Anthropic to pull Claude Fable 5 days after launch, and Anthropic shut the model off worldwide within about 90 minutes because it could not verify nationality in real time.
  • The letter argues that open weights help organizations control their own data, adapt models to their needs, deploy them where required, avoid single points of failure, and improve AI safety and security through transparency.

Products: kimi-k3, claude-fable-5

Vendors: nvidia, microsoft, meta, google, ibm, dell, mistral, hugging-face, mozilla, linux-foundation, moonshot-ai, anthropic, openai, amazon, crowdstrike, palo-alto-networks

item.title: GitHub and PyPI Add Time-Based Defenses Against Package Supply Chain Attacks
item.content:encoded:
Window: 26 Jul 14:00 → 26 Jul 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

GitHub, PyPI add time-absed defenses against supply chain attacks — Should Read

GitHub and PyPI are adding time-based safeguards to reduce supply-chain risk: Dependabot now waits 72 hours before suggesting new dependency updates, and PyPI blocks adding files to releases after 14 days. The goal is to limit how quickly malicious or compromised packages can spread before detection and cleanup.

  • GitHub and PyPI introduced time-based defenses intended to protect against supply-chain attacks and limit their impact.
  • Dependabot now uses a default three-day cooldown before issuing package update pull requests, with users able to configure a shorter or longer delay.
  • GitHub said the three-day delay is meant to reduce the risk of automatically adopting newly published malicious packages while still allowing projects to keep up with upgrades.
  • PyPI now rejects new files uploaded to package releases more than 14 days after the release was published.
  • PyPI said the 14-day cutoff is intended to prevent attackers with compromised publishing tokens or workflows from poisoning old, trusted releases.

Technologies: source-control, package-registry

Products: dependabot, pypi, npm, github

Vendors: github, pypi

item.title: DKIM- and DMARC-Passing Reply-To Hijack Targets $97,500 Wire Payment
item.content:encoded:
Window: 26 Jul 10:00 → 26 Jul 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

DKIM and DMARC Passed. The $97,500 Wire Was Fraud. — Should Read

A $97,500 wire-fraud email passed DKIM and DMARC because it was sent through a legitimate institution’s authorized mail stream, but a mismatched Reply-To redirected responses to the attacker. The key takeaway is that email authentication proves domain control, not that a payment request is legitimate, so high-value transactions still require out-of-band verification.

  • An accounts-payable team received an invoice demanding a same-day $97,500 ACH or wire payment that was framed as a reply to an already-approved item.
  • The message passed DKIM and DMARC, was signed by a real federal cultural and research institution’s own mail stream through SendGrid, and received a Microsoft composite authentication score of 100.
  • The fraud depended on a mismatched Reply-To address, mahalaxmitraders@waareepartners[.]com, which used the trusted display name but pointed replies to an unrelated domain controlled by the attacker.
  • The email included a SendGrid open-tracking pixel that could confirm when the target rendered the message.
  • IRONSCALES quarantined the message across all four affected mailboxes after its Adaptive AI analyst, Themis, flagged the first-time sender, Reply-To mismatch, urgent large-dollar request, and related reputation signals.

Technologies: email-security

Products: themis, sendgrid

Vendors: ironscales, sendgrid, microsoft

item.title: Steam ClickFix Posts Push PowerShell-Installed XMRig Cryptominers
item.content:encoded:
Window: 25 Jul 22:00 → 26 Jul 02:00 UTC (4 hours)

Steam forum ClickFix attacks infect gamers with XMRig cryptominers — Should Read

Attackers are abusing Steam discussion forums with fake “fixes” that tell users to run PowerShell commands, which secretly install the XMRig cryptominer with persistence and Microsoft Defender exclusions. Users should not run forum-provided commands and should check for the C:\Windows\Background folder, XMRig scheduled tasks, and Defender exclusions if they did.

  • Threat actors are creating random Steam accounts to post replies that appear to offer fixes for game crashes, lost inventory items, and other technical issues.
  • The malicious replies instruct users to open PowerShell as an administrator and run a command that quietly downloads and launches an XMRig miner executable.
  • The PowerShell script masquerades as a Windows optimization utility named "msf utility \\ PC Opt" and displays fake maintenance progress messages to appear legitimate.
  • When run with administrator privileges, the script creates C:\Windows\Background, adds that path as a Microsoft Defender exclusion, downloads a payload from msfconfig[.]icu, and installs it as C:\Windows\Background\system.exe.
  • The malware creates a scheduled task named "XMRig-[computer name]" to launch system.exe with SYSTEM privileges every time Windows starts.

Technologies: operating-system, antivirus, firewall

Products: steam, xmrig, powershell, windows, microsoft-defender, windows-firewall

Vendors: valve, microsoft, xmrig

item.title: SourTrade Malvertising Assembles Per-Victim Windows Malware Inside Browsers
item.content:encoded:
Window: 25 Jul 18:00 → 25 Jul 22:00 UTC (4 hours)

Malvertising Sends Malware in Pieces, Then Makes the Browser Build the Executable — Should Read

The SourTrade malvertising campaign impersonates trading and crypto services and makes victims’ browsers assemble unique Windows executables from pieces, limiting simple hash-based detection. Defenders should focus on the full delivery chain, including cloaked landing pages, /config requests, secondary runtime downloads, and ServiceWorker-based file delivery.

  • Confiant said the SourTrade malvertising operation has operated since late 2024 and impersonated TradingView, Solana, and Luno to target retail traders and cryptocurrency investors across 12 countries in 25 languages.
  • The campaign’s landing pages fingerprint visitors, show suspected researchers and bots an empty page, and serve selected targets a convincing copy of the impersonated service.
  • The delivery chain registers a ServiceWorker, builds a SharedWorker from JavaScript embedded in the page, requests a /config file, retrieves a clean Bun runtime from a secondary domain, and assembles a Windows executable in the browser from supplied components.
  • Confiant reported that rotating the seed and size in each /config response can give each victim a different assembled file hash while retaining the executable payload code.
  • The article states that there is no software patch to apply and that defenders should examine the full chain from ad referral and cloaked landing page through the /config request, secondary-domain runtime fetch, and ServiceWorker download.

Technologies: browser

Products: bun, javascriptcore, streamsaver.js, serviceworker, sharedworker

Vendors: confiant, oven-sh, apple, streamsaver-project, bitdefender, checkpoint, withsecure

item.title: In-Browser Malware Malvertising Targets Crypto Users; ShinyHunters Leaks Fuel Sextortion
item.content:encoded:
Window: 25 Jul 14:00 → 25 Jul 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Malicious sites use JavaScript to build malware in browser memory — Should Read

A large malvertising campaign is using fake Solana, Luno, and TradingView sites to make victims’ browsers assemble unique malware executables in memory, helping evade network and static detection. Crypto investors and traders should avoid sponsored downloads and only install apps from official sources after verifying signatures.

  • A massive malvertising campaign uses fake Solana, Luno, and TradingView webpages with malicious JavaScript that instructs browsers to assemble malware directly in memory.
  • The operation has been active since late 2024, is localized to 25 languages in 12 countries, and primarily targets retail traders and crypto investors in Asia Pacific and Latin America.
  • Confiant says the pages register a service worker and use a SharedWorker to request a randomized “/config” response so each session can build a malware file with a unique hash.
  • The technique avoids transmitting a finished malware file over the network, making detection less likely and analysis more challenging.
  • Users engaged in financial or cryptocurrency activities are advised to avoid downloading apps from social media advertisements or sponsored search results and to verify installers from official company websites.

Products: javascript, reactjs, service-worker, sharedworker, bun, streamsaver, mark-of-the-web

Vendors: confiant, bitdefender, solana, luno, tradingview, github, meta

ShinyHunters data leaks fuel $2,000 sextortion email scam — Should Read

Scammers are using email addresses from ShinyHunters-leaked breaches to send fake sextortion emails demanding $2,000 in Bitcoin. There is no evidence recipients’ devices were hacked, and victims should not pay or respond.

  • Threat actors are using email addresses exposed in data breaches leaked by ShinyHunters to send sextortion emails demanding $2,000 in Bitcoin.
  • BleepingComputer saw leaked data from the Amtrak, Hallmark, Substack, Betterment, CarGurus, ADT, Panera Bread, and McGraw Hill breaches used in the campaign.
  • The emails claim to be from ShinyHunters and falsely state that attackers compromised recipients’ devices, accessed cameras and microphones, and recorded them visiting adult websites.
  • BleepingComputer contacted ShinyHunters, and the extortion group denied involvement in the sextortion email campaign.
  • Recipients are advised not to pay the ransom or respond to the sender, because there is no indication the sender accessed their devices or personal activity.

item.title: Fastjson CVE-2026-16723, GitLab RCE PoC, and Cl0p PTC Exploitation Drive Threat Activity
item.content:encoded:
Window: 25 Jul 10:00 → 25 Jul 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

Fastjson 1.x RCE Vulnerability Targeted in Attacks With No Patched Available — Must Read

Attackers are targeting CVE-2026-16723, a critical Fastjson 1.x RCE affecting certain Spring Boot fat-JAR deployments, and no patched Fastjson 1.x release was available as of July 25. Organizations should migrate to Fastjson2 or enable SafeMode/use 1.2.83_noneautotype as a mitigation.

  • Security firms ThreatBook and Imperva say attackers are targeting CVE-2026-16723, a critical remote code execution flaw in Alibaba's Fastjson library for Java.
  • The confirmed vulnerability chain requires Fastjson 1.2.68 through 1.2.83, a Spring Boot executable fat-JAR, a network-reachable path that sends attacker-controlled JSON to an affected parser, and SafeMode left disabled.
  • Alibaba had not released a fixed Fastjson 1.x version as of July 25, and organizations that cannot migrate immediately should enable SafeMode or use com.alibaba:fastjson:1.2.83_noneautotype.
  • Alibaba lists migration to Fastjson2 as the long-term fix, and the article states Fastjson2 is not affected because it does not use the same resource-probing or annotation-based trust path.
  • ThreatBook reported in-the-wild exploitation, while Imperva reported activity against several sectors, but neither vendor published attack counts, raw requests, execution evidence, named victims, or confirmed compromises.

Products: fastjson, fastjson2, spring-boot, jdk, apache-tomcat, eclipse-jetty

Vendors: alibaba, threatbook, imperva, fearsoff-cybersecurity

Cl0p Affiliates Target Internet-Exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM with Unauthenticated RCE — Must Read

Cl0p-linked attackers are exploiting internet-facing PTC Windchill and FlexPLM systems by chaining a FlexPLM information disclosure flaw with a Windchill unauthenticated RCE to deploy JSP web shells and steal sensitive engineering/design data. Organizations using these products should urgently investigate exposure, apply mitigations or patches, and check for the published IoCs.

  • Threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware campaign are exploiting flaws in internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM deployments as part of a new data extortion campaign.
  • The attackers chain a pre-authentication information disclosure in the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint with a server-side flaw in the Windchill login servlet to enable unauthenticated remote code execution and deployment of hex-named JSP web shells under /Windchill/login/.
  • After gaining initial access, the attackers have been observed enumerating file systems, staging engineering and design data, and conducting double extortion data theft against manufacturing, automotive, aerospace, and retail targets.
  • PTC said it has received continued reports of heightened threat activity and warned that unknown attackers are exploiting the vulnerability to deploy JSP web shells against susceptible systems.
  • Ransom-ISAC shared four indicators-of-compromise IP addresses that match those shared by PTC: 216.152.148.54, 216.152.151.204, 104.243.35.63, and 5.180.41.35.

Products: ptc-windchill, flexplm

Vendors: ptc

Researcher Publishes GitLab RCE PoC Letting Authenticated Users Run Commands as Git — Should Read

Researchers published a working proof-of-concept for a GitLab RCE chain that lets any authenticated user with project push access run commands as the git user on unpatched self-managed instances. The flaw was fixed in GitLab 18.10.8, 18.11.5, and 19.0.2, but it was not initially labeled as a security fix, so operators should verify and upgrade immediately.

  • Security researchers at depthfirst published working exploit code on July 24 for a GitLab flaw that GitLab patched on June 10.
  • Any authenticated user who can push to a project can exploit the issue by committing crafted Jupyter notebooks and opening their commit diffs to ultimately run commands as the git user.
  • GitLab did not list the Oj 3.17.3 update as a security fix in the June 10 patch release, and the issue has no CVE, CVSS score, or mention of the notebook-diff chain.
  • Affected versions include GitLab CE/EE 15.2.0 to 18.10.7, 18.11.0 to 18.11.4, and 19.0.0 to 19.0.1, as well as Oj gem versions 3.13.0 to 3.17.1.
  • The article says operators should upgrade to GitLab 18.10.8, 18.11.5, or 19.0.2, and that no workaround is offered for those who cannot upgrade.

The Phish Zoom Signed With Its Own DKIM Key — Should Read

Attackers abused Zoom’s own sign-in email template by placing a PayPal callback scam in the account name field, causing Zoom to DKIM-sign a genuine-looking phishing message that passed DMARC. The key takeaway is that valid email authentication proves origin and integrity, not that the content is safe.

  • An attacker set a Zoom account name to a scam script about a fabricated $986.37 PayPal auto-debit and then triggered a Zoom sign-in verification email.
  • Zoom rendered the attacker-controlled account name into its standard sign-in-code email template and signed the finished message with its production DKIM key for zoom.us.
  • The resent message passed DMARC because the Zoom DKIM signature was aligned, even though the envelope domain mailjetstream.com had no SPF record and no relationship to Zoom's mail platform.
  • The only attack payload was the callback number +1-805-600-1572, with no malicious link or attachment for URL sandboxes, attachment detonation, or domain-reputation engines to analyze.
  • The article states that a valid DKIM signature proves the signing key and message integrity, but not whether the message content is safe or trustworthy.

Products: zoom, dkim, dmarc, spf, microsoft-365, cloudflare, ironscales-adaptive-ai, mitre-attack

Fastjson 1.x RCE Vulnerability Targeted in Attacks With No Patched Available — Must Read

Attackers are exploiting a critical Fastjson 1.x RCE flaw in certain Spring Boot fat-JAR applications, and no patched Fastjson 1.x release is available yet. Organizations should enable SafeMode or use the restricted 1.2.83_noneautotype build while migrating to Fastjson2.

  • Security firms ThreatBook and Imperva say attackers are targeting CVE-2026-16723, a critical remote code execution flaw in Alibaba’s Fastjson 1.x JSON library for Java.
  • The confirmed exploit chain requires Fastjson 1.2.68 through 1.2.83, a Spring Boot executable fat-JAR, a network-reachable path that passes attacker-controlled JSON to an affected parser, and SafeMode left disabled.
  • Alibaba had not released a fixed Fastjson 1.x version as of July 25, and recommended enabling SafeMode, using com.alibaba:fastjson:1.2.83_noneautotype, or migrating to Fastjson2.
  • Alibaba’s advisory said the flaw requires no AutoType enablement and no classpath gadget, and the maintainers verified the chain on Spring Boot 2.x, 3.x, and 4.x with JDK 8, 11, 17, and 21.
  • ThreatBook and Imperva reported observed exploitation activity, but neither vendor published attack counts, raw requests, execution evidence, named victims, or confirmed compromises.

Products: fastjson, fastjson2, spring-boot, jdk, apache-tomcat, jetty, maven-central

Vendors: alibaba, threatbook, imperva, fears-off-cybersecurity

Cl0p Affiliates Target Internet-Exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM with Unauthenticated RCE — Must Read

Cl0p-linked attackers are exploiting internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM systems by chaining a FlexPLM information disclosure flaw with a Windchill RCE to deploy JSP web shells and steal sensitive engineering and product data. Organizations using these products should urgently investigate exposure, apply mitigations, and check for the reported indicators of compromise.

  • Threat actors linked to the Cl0p ransomware campaign are exploiting flaws in internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM deployments as part of a data extortion campaign.
  • Attackers chain a pre-authentication information disclosure in the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint with a server-side flaw in the Windchill login servlet to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy hex-named JSP web shells under /Windchill/login/.
  • The campaign has targeted manufacturing, automotive, aerospace, and retail sectors, with attackers enumerating file systems, staging engineering and design data, and carrying out double extortion data theft.
  • PTC said it has received continued reports of heightened threat activity and warned that unknown attackers are exploiting the vulnerability to deploy JSP web shells against susceptible systems.
  • Ransom-ISAC shared four IP addresses as indicators of compromise: 216.152.148.54, 216.152.151.204, 104.243.35.63, and 5.180.41.35.

Products: ptc-windchill, flexplm

Vendors: ptc

Researcher Publishes GitLab RCE PoC Letting Authenticated Users Run Commands as Git — Must Read

Researchers published exploit code for a GitLab remote code execution flaw that lets any authenticated user with project push access run commands as the git user on unpatched self-managed instances. Operators should urgently upgrade to GitLab 18.10.8, 18.11.5, or 19.0.2 and verify the version inside the Webservice image, since the fix was not originally labeled as a security patch.

  • Security researchers at depthfirst published working exploit code on July 24 for a GitLab flaw that GitLab patched on June 10.
  • The flaw lets any authenticated user who can push to a project run commands as the git account on an unpatched self-managed GitLab 18.11.3 server.
  • The exploit chain uses crafted Jupyter notebooks opened in a commit diff to leak a heap pointer, locate libraries in memory, and trigger a payload through two Oj memory corruption bugs.
  • GitLab listed the Oj 3.17.3 bump under bug fixes rather than in the security-fix table, with no CVE, CVSS score, or mention of the notebook-diff chain.
  • Affected users are advised to upgrade to GitLab 18.10.8, 18.11.5, or 19.0.2, and the article says neither GitLab nor depthfirst offers a workaround for those who cannot upgrade.

Products: gitlab-ce-ee, oj, ipynbdiff, puma, ruby, jupyter-notebook, helm, gitlab-operator, gitlab-webservice, jemalloc

Vendors: gitlab, depthfirst, oj

DevMan RaaS Portal Centralizes Payload Builds, Victim Management, and Affiliate Payouts — Should Read

PRODAFT says the DevMan ransomware group has built a centralized RaaS portal to manage payload creation, victims, affiliate teams, chats, deadlines, and payouts, showing a more formalized and tightly controlled operation. The platform supports Windows, Linux, ESXi, and alleged SCADA-focused lockers, with affiliates encouraged to target critical infrastructure outside restricted regions.

  • PRODAFT reported that the DevMan ransomware-as-a-service operation maintains a dedicated web portal for affiliates to build payloads, manage victim records and chats, oversee earnings, and handle payouts.
  • DevMan first appeared in April 2025 as an affiliate for Qilin, DragonForce, Apos, and RansomHub before moving to its own ransomware-as-a-service operation, and Vectra AI said its locker has a clear DragonForce lineage.
  • The third version of the DevMan platform, released in January 2026, added structured victim records, lifecycle states, team creation, invitation controls, per-victim build options, deadline tracking, revenue fields, and shared operational access.
  • Ransomware.Live statistics cited in the article say DevMan has claimed 184 victims, with nearly 50 in the United States and the most targeted sectors including technology, healthcare, financial services, professional services, and government.
  • The latest DevMan portal allows affiliates to create lockers for Windows, ESXi, or Linux, and PRODAFT found the Windows version includes functions for privilege checking, security-control impairment, recovery inhibition, event log clearing, lateral movement, and multi-threaded encryption.

Technologies: operating-system, hypervisor, ics-scada, remote-access, mfa, backup

Malvertising Sends Malware in Pieces, Then Makes the Browser Build the Executable — Should Read

The SourTrade malvertising campaign impersonates trading and crypto services and makes victims’ browsers assemble unique Windows executables from pieces, limiting simple hash-based detection. Defenders should focus on the full delivery chain, including cloaked landing pages, /config requests, secondary runtime downloads, and ServiceWorker-based file delivery.

  • Confiant said the SourTrade malvertising operation has operated since late 2024 and impersonated TradingView, Solana, and Luno to target retail traders and cryptocurrency investors across 12 countries in 25 languages.
  • The campaign’s landing pages fingerprint visitors, show suspected researchers and bots an empty page, and serve selected targets a convincing copy of the impersonated service.
  • The delivery chain registers a ServiceWorker, builds a SharedWorker from JavaScript embedded in the page, requests a /config file, retrieves a clean Bun runtime from a secondary domain, and assembles a Windows executable in the browser from supplied components.
  • Confiant reported that rotating the seed and size in each /config response can give each victim a different assembled file hash while retaining the executable payload code.
  • The article states that there is no software patch to apply and that defenders should examine the full chain from ad referral and cloaked landing page through the /config request, secondary-domain runtime fetch, and ServiceWorker download.

Technologies: browser

CTM360 reports that insurance phishing has evolved from simple credential theft into real-time account hijacking, with attackers using Google Ads, disposable hosting, and live OTP interception to access victim accounts during the same session. The key takeaway is that defenders must look beyond phishing sites and monitor attacker infrastructure, workflows, and authentication behavior.

  • The campaign used sponsored Google advertisements for insurance quotations, renewals, or price comparisons as a primary delivery mechanism, redirecting victims to phishing websites that closely resembled genuine insurance providers.
  • The operation reused infrastructure across multiple insurance brands and primarily targeted Saudi Arabia, with additional activity observed across Europe, the United States, and India.
  • CTM360 identified a previously undocumented phishing kit called InsureOTP Kit that supports live session management, real-time data collection, backend administration, Telegram Bot integrations, and live OTP handling.
  • The article states that defenders should monitor for paid advertisements abusing their brands, newly registered lookalike domains, disposable cloud-hosted phishing infrastructure, and authentication patterns that indicate real-time OTP interception.

Steam forum ClickFix attacks infect gamers with XMRig cryptominers — Should Read

Attackers are abusing Steam discussion forums with fake “fixes” that tell users to run PowerShell commands, which secretly install the XMRig cryptominer with persistence and Microsoft Defender exclusions. Users should not run forum-provided commands and should check for the C:\Windows\Background folder, XMRig scheduled tasks, and Defender exclusions if they did.

  • Threat actors are creating random Steam accounts to post replies that appear to offer fixes for game crashes, lost inventory items, and other technical issues.
  • The malicious replies instruct users to open PowerShell as an administrator and run a command that quietly downloads and launches an XMRig miner executable.
  • The PowerShell script masquerades as a Windows optimization utility named "msf utility \\ PC Opt" and displays fake maintenance progress messages to appear legitimate.
  • When run with administrator privileges, the script creates C:\Windows\Background, adds that path as a Microsoft Defender exclusion, downloads a payload from msfconfig[.]icu, and installs it as C:\Windows\Background\system.exe.
  • The malware creates a scheduled task named "XMRig-[computer name]" to launch system.exe with SYSTEM privileges every time Windows starts.

Technologies: operating-system, antivirus, firewall

Products: steam, xmrig, powershell, windows, microsoft-defender, windows-firewall

Vendors: valve, microsoft, xmrig

ShinyHunters data leaks fuel $2,000 sextortion email scam — Should Read

Scammers are using email addresses from ShinyHunters-leaked breaches to send fake sextortion emails demanding $2,000 in Bitcoin. There is no evidence recipients’ devices were hacked, and victims should not pay or respond.

  • Threat actors are using email addresses exposed in data breaches leaked by ShinyHunters to send sextortion emails demanding $2,000 in Bitcoin.
  • BleepingComputer saw leaked data from the Amtrak, Hallmark, Substack, Betterment, CarGurus, ADT, Panera Bread, and McGraw Hill breaches used in the campaign.
  • The emails claim to be from ShinyHunters and falsely state that attackers compromised recipients’ devices, accessed cameras and microphones, and recorded them visiting adult websites.
  • BleepingComputer contacted ShinyHunters, and the extortion group denied involvement in the sextortion email campaign.
  • Recipients are advised not to pay the ransom or respond to the sender, because there is no indication the sender accessed their devices or personal activity.

OpenAI confirms ChatGPT is down worldwide — May Read

OpenAI confirmed a worldwide outage affecting ChatGPT, Codex, and multiple API endpoints, preventing users from loading chats or sending messages. The company said it applied a fix, and services were reported fully recovered after about 50 minutes.

  • ChatGPT experienced a major worldwide outage starting at approximately 5 AM ET, affecting users including those in the United States and Europe.
  • Affected users were unable to load chats, including previous conversations, and could not send messages due to "too many concurrent requests" errors.
  • The outage also affected OpenAI's Codex coding platform and the OpenAI API, with as many as 12 API endpoints listed as having issues on OpenAI's status page.
  • OpenAI acknowledged the issue on its status page at 5:30 AM ET and said it was investigating the affected services.
  • OpenAI said it applied a fix, and ChatGPT was reported fully recovered by 6 AM ET after an outage lasting almost 50 minutes.

Products: chatgpt, codex, openai-api

Vendors: openai
